notation.meaning: Wage bill paid to college workers
Total and college wage bill in industry $i$
Share of high-ability workers in each education group

blocks.md: A shift-share decomposition splits a change in an overall share into two sources. Suppose the share of the wage bill paid to college graduates rises. That could happen because industries that hire many graduates grew — a shift in the mix of industries — or because each industry started hiring more graduates. The decomposition measures how much of the change comes from each, using simple accounting with no assumptions about causes.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It is a fast first look at whether a change is driven by the economy's composition or by changes within its parts — but it describes, it does not explain.
An **accounting** split of a change in an aggregate share into a part from shifts in the mix of units (between) and a part from changes inside units (within).
Industries $i$. Wage bill $WB_t$, wage bill paid to college workers $WB_{Ht}$. The college wage-bill share is a weighted average of industry college shares:
college intensity of industry $i$ × industry $i$'s share of the total wage bill.
Bars are averages over the two periods. With averaged weights the decomposition is **exact**: $\Delta(ab) = \bar{a}\,\Delta b + \bar{b}\,\Delta a$.

- **Between**: college-intensive industries grow.
- **Within**: industries become more college-intensive.
1967–2017: college wage-bill share rises from ≈20% to 54.7% (+34.7 pp). Between ≈ 1.1 pp; **within ≈ 33.6 pp**. See [College Wage Bill Share 1967-2017](note:college-wage-bill-share-1967-2017).

sections.heading: Why a causal reading is dangerous

blocks.md: The lecture flags it without elaborating. The standard reasons:

- **Supply moves the share too.** A wage-bill share is price × quantity. More college graduates lower the premium and lead *every* industry to hire more of them, which appears as "within" with no demand shift at all.
- **Within is not the same as technology.** Trade and outsourcing of low-skill tasks *inside* an industry also show up as within.
- **Granularity.** Finer industry definitions move change from within to between.

[Shift-Share Exposure](note:shift-share-exposure) uses "shift-share" for a different object: a unit's share-weighted average of sector-level shocks (the Bartik structure), used to predict how regions or factors are hit by trade or demand shocks. This note's decomposition is an accounting split of a change in an aggregate share.

- [Within- and Between-Group Inequality](note:within-and-between-group-inequality) — same logic, different object
